Senses.Explanation: After light and scene are both gone, or after true and false no longer differ, the surviving question is “what then is it?”, and the records also raise Panshan Baoji’s use of that question. Foyan Qingyuan asks it after removing empty space, mirror, light, and scene in a memorial address. Letan Hongying asks it after saying light and scene are both absent. In the Sikong Benjing exchange, Chan Master An asks it after true and false have been made indistinguishable; Benjing answers that calling it any thing is itself false. Panshan Baoji asks the same words after saying that the three realms and six paths are only mental constructions; later records raise his saying as an old case.

Senses.Explanation: Chan speakers reach for the phrase (掩室摩竭, the closed room in Magadha) as the name of the founder's own withdrawal into silence, and they almost always set it beside Vimalakirti's shut mouth in Vaishali — Huqiu Shaolong, Liangting Jingting, Suru Honghan, and Yongjue Yuanxian among them. Shaolong files it with the other founding devices — the nine years of wall-gazing, the night crossing at Huangmei — and then inspects the whole set into mere reckoning; Yuanxian confesses that this essence not even he can point out, and that Śākyamuni himself could only close the room over it; and a questioner auditing Liangting Jingting's conduct receives the phrase alone as the answer to why he declines invitations. In his own record Huqiu Shaolong opens the address for appointing stewards with the pair — the closed room in Magadha, the shut mouth in Vaishali, nine years facing the wall, the night crossing at Huangmei — and then rules on the inventory: inspected point by point, it all turns into reckoning; the sun needs no fire to be hot. In another hall address in the same record he states the pair's own grammar, with the graphs running the other way: in these cases principle was what steered the spirit, and so the mouth fell silent by it — not that there was no eloquence; eloquence cannot say it. Furong Daokai weighs the room twice. In the hall he runs the transmission line — before the Buddha of Infinite Sound no stages apply, after Dipankara the mind passes to mind, ancestor succeeding ancestor — and rules the Magadha closed room seemingly-so-but-not, before the wheel's three turnings in the Deer Park. In an assembly address kept by the Lamp Compendium he tells the story behind the room: the yellow-faced old man himself knew his fault and closed the room; and whoever takes that for the ultimate has already cut himself on the blade, and now smears a greasy hat onto his own head. Liangting Jingting puts the phrase to work as an answer. A questioner audits his ten vows one by one — why, when buddhas appear in the world for the one great matter, does the abbot not accept invitations? — and Liangting answers with the phrase alone: the closed room in Magadha. Later in the same record he dismisses the pair from discussion — Vaishali's shut mouth, Magadha's closed room, no need anymore to raise them — and at once turns it back on the questioner: but in days to come, with what will you help people?. Tiantong Rujing raises the pair as the two old cases: in Magadha's closed room the old foreigner split open the crown of his head; in Vaishali's silent city Vimalakirti ruined his own story-line; to raise the two old cases of high antiquity is to issue a beam of authority for this morning. The late masters test the pair and set it aside. Shanhui Huan, taking the seat at a small courtyard, lists what came down from above — the Magadha closed room, the Shaolin wall-gazing, the Linji gate-wind, the Yangqi vein — none of it applies here. Tianran Hanshi, re-ascending the seat after six years hidden in the wild mountains, grants the pair a rank only to negate it: certainly not the mysterious-marvelous pivot, nor does it fall among the ranks of achievement. Suru Honghan at the year-end whisk-turn address: even if Śākyamuni closed the room and Vimalakirti shut the mouth, seen with the true eye it all turns into extra fuss. Yushan Shangsi, opening a new abbot's hall, has Śākyamuni and Vimalakirti display their powers — the closed room setting countless devas confusing one another, the silence arguing the thirty-two worthies to a finish — and then rules both of them, on inspection, waves without wind against his own thatched gate. Azi Jinwu plays the pair for comedy at a precept address: with the room closed and the mouth shut, Manjushri and Samantabhadra share one shrine and still cannot cover their ears; only the elder Upali, riding the occasion, comes out to say that with the morning star not yet risen there is no buddha's name and no being's name, so why not expound the Vinaya. Yongjue Yuanxian, answering a demand to point the essence out directly, binds himself and the founders together: this essence not only Yuanxian cannot point out — even old Śākyamuni could only close the room in Magadha, old Vimalakirti only shut the mouth in Vaishali, for there are no words to say it and no principle to state it.

Senses.Explanation: To cover one's ears while stealing a bell is to hide from oneself the noise that exposes one's own act. Muzhou Daoming says a pious-sounding account resembles covering the ears while stealing a bell. Yuan'an Feng joins it to 'clutching the stolen goods and crying injustice'; Hanyue Fazang calls his interlocutor an ear-covering bell thief and then strikes him. Yuanjie Ying forbids the move, while Konggu Daocheng applies it to people who imagine they have deceived others. Chan usage preserves the self-defeating concealment: the attempted evasion itself advertises what the named critic exposes.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names devices put out to catch or draw someone: words, gestures, and inherited formulations. Ying’an Tanhua includes Deshan's blows, Linji's shouts, and patriarchal devices in this class. Yunmen Wenyan lists finger snaps, coughs, gestures, hammers, whisks, and circles, then says all are hooks and lines and have not yet touched the words 'the teaching.' Shantang Xun extends the warning to inherited sayings and technical formulas: all can catch or lead, but none is the student's own affair.
